items.title: The very second apron that paved the way for their title seeks to destroy the Knicks
items.author: Michael Zeno
items.content:
Sports are cyclical. It’s very rare for a team to stay on top for a prolonged period of time, just the same as it’s rare for a team to stay in the doldrums for a long time. Smart organizations can keep championship windows open, and dumb organizations can keep shooting themselves in the foot, but in every sport, the bill eventually comes due.

The second apron, an invention of the latest CBA, has been the NBA’s attempt to speed up the cycle. They don’t want teams like the Warriors spending five years at the top of the sport with their all-time collection of talent. They want championship windows to be shorter, but also more volatile. It’s like a conveyor belt; they want these teams to all get a taste of glory before going back to the hunt.

As the current NBA champions, the Knicks are the latest team to fight a battle with the second apron. James Dolan says he does not want to exceed it, something that very few teams have done since it was introduced. They find themselves with a core that wants to be compensated as champions, but have a finite amount of money to get there.

It’s easy to curse the second apron for what they’re doing to muddy up the Knicks’ title defense and beyond, but in doing that, we have to remember that the construction and reason behind this team even reaching the mountaintop was the second apron.

The Minnesota Timberwolves were coming off a trip to the Western Conference Finals, but faced a massive crisis entering the 2024-25 season with their financial table. Some players needed extensions, some players had massive raises kicking in, and they were doomed to spend the season above the second apron. You can spend one year there and survive, but doing two or more years there is a death sentence. Hence, they needed to shed long-term salary.

That’s how Karl-Anthony Towns became a Knick.

The Boston Celtics were the type of unstoppable superteam that the league looked to avoid in 2023-24, boasting a starting five full of players who could create their own shot and hold their own defensively, an extremely rare blend. All of that was bolstered by an elite coach who maximized offensive efficiency with the three-pointer.

It was expensive to keep that team together the following season, and they did it in the second apron, but they knew they had to make changes after 2024-25 to avoid dooming themselves long term with a still-young superstar in Jayson Tatum. When the Knicks took out a bruised, battered Celtics team that May, they offloaded Kristaps Porzingis and Jrue Holiday and lost Al Horford and Luke Kornet to free agency, destroying that unstoppable ceiling and paving the way for the Knicks to take their place at the top of the totem pole.

The second apron unraveled the Celtics and Timberwolves, feeding a Knicks team that was excellently built and simply waited until their time to strike. Now, the Robin Hood nature of the second apron has come around to collect from the champs.

Karl-Anthony Towns wants an extension. Deuce McBride wants an extension. Josh Hart (who’s less of a priority due to a team option in 2027-28) wants an extension. Jalen Brunson is due at least $290 million down the road in a future extension (and could be up to $411 million). There’s not enough room under the second apron to keep them all happy.

The second apron already threw a right hook at the Knicks’ underbelly by forcing them to let go of Mitchell Robinson, but now they could come back and take McBride from them next season (or force them to trade him). The desire to keep the band together has caused a lowballing of Towns, something that is openly frustrating him in the media.

And now, we’re getting reports that both he and Hart could be trade chips in February if we can’t get a deal done? What happened to all the good vibes???

No matter how much “power of friendship” you have, money is the universal divider. I’m not calling Towns greedy for wanting to make more than residential losing players, Trae Young and De’Aaron Fox, but I’m also not going to call the Knicks prudish.

The second apron is extremely restrictive and, at most, you can exceed it one time before its vice grips start to sink in. I’m not sure if Dolan knows that fact, but if he does, you have to be very careful with how you use it.

It unfortunately seems like this will be a distraction for the Knicks in their title defense with how rigid the two sides seem to be. As much as it sucks, that’s the second apron.

It steals from the rich and gives to the poor.

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Definitely heartbreaking’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
The New York Knicks officially unofficially played basketball yesterday, and I can’t be happier about an opponent’s win.

As Russell said in his Scenes, we’ll give them belt when it counts, but for now, all I needed was some Orange and Blue hoops in my screen.

Here’s the latest from NYK world coming off Monday’s loss. Get well soon, Huk.

On playing everyone available in the preseason opener:

“Everybody’s been busting their behind in camp. Everybody’s good people, and it’s our first game. So I’m gonna play everybody. Twenty guys. Jose’s not playing.”

On the Knicks’ lack of physicality in the preseason loss to Philadelphia:

“Most of it, I was okay with (the performance). I just listed things that I saw that I know we can be better at. What bothers me is our lack of physicality throughout the ballgame, and that’s the whole roster, up and down. We weren’t great on the ball physically, and we weren’t great with our defensive positioning physically.

“That I’m concerned about, and I don’t wanna see it happen (again). The rest of the stuff, it’s coach-talk. It’s real, but it’s coach-talk that we’ll clean up watching film and all that stuff. I can’t help with the physicality. That they got to find it individually, which will then turn into collectively. That’s how you find minutes. That’s how you make the team. That’s how you contribute.”

On evaluating the Knicks’ options at center:

“I think just it’s just kind of gut feel. And then we’ll look at production because they’re gonna probably give us different levels of protection in different areas. Tony is just a really smart guy that has a great feel for the game, and when you watch him play, they’re not necessarily sexy, but he’s extremely efficient, and then there are times when it’s like, ‘Oh, my God, he kicked our ass [in the past].

“When you look at Wiseman, he’s younger, he’s a little more raw, he’s a vertical threat. He’s one of the best runners I’ve been around. You can see and feel his length and his athleticism and his potential.

“Then when you look at Drew, just a toughness about him, and you know what you’re gonna get, not tonight, but every fricking night that you go out there, ’cause he’s got a great feel, a great sense of toughness about him, and again, he’s not afraid to do anything against anybody, and his belief is at a pretty high level.

“So they’ll all initially bring something a little bit different, and we’ll just see, at the end of the day, if any of them, in terms of the center spot, fit well enough to be on our team.”

On Mikal Bridges attacking the rim:

“It’s great. He’s long, athletic and smart. He can finish at the rim. He’s capable of playing off of two feet and making a spray because he has a tremendous feel for the game.”

On creating more offensive opportunities for OG Anunoby:

“We have to try and put him in those positions a bit more, but he also has to have a good feel of what he wants and get to his spots. With him being in the system for a year, he’s got a better feel. … We also have a better feel on how to use him. I don’t call a lot of plays, and now he can find the small areas where he can be aggressive offensively. … His natural ability, especially with how hard he works, is showing.”

On wishing Ariel Hukporti a speedy recovery:

“We hope Ariel — whatever is wrong with him — he has a speedy recovery and he’s back on the floor. You hate to see anybody go down with an injury, but especially somebody who is a caliber person who Ariel is.”

On the 76ers’ roster and their status as an Eastern Conference contender:

“You look at their roster, man, it’s just loaded: multiple-time All-Star, multiple-time All-Star, multiple-time All-Star, MVP candidate, MVP candidate, MVP candidate. I remember back in the day, Pop said — when I was an assistant for him — there is a change from having two All-Stars on your team to having three. He brought it to our attention as a staff. He was like, you made at least three NBA All-Stars, and not just one-offs, but perennial All-Stars to go win a championship.

“And this is when we were going against Kobe [Bryant] and Shaq[uille O’Neal] and their [Lakers] team and all that.

“You look at this [Philly] team here, and they’ve got as many All-Stars or guys of that nature as they had in Miami when LeBron was down there. So they’re definitely a deep team, a talented team. Nick Nurse does a phenomenal job. He’s a championship-level coach, and they’re definitely going to be one of the teams that are contending in the East.

“In my opinion, it just got harder for everybody with the team that they assembled here.”

On LeBron James reaching his 24th NBA season:

“The first thing, I guess like year 24 is insane. It’s unheard of. It’s not human. People talk about Wemby being not human because of what he can do for his size. You got to throw LeBron in that category because of his durability and still doing it at the age that he has at a high level. It’s amazing to watch, but if there’s anybody that’s going to do it, he’s going to do it because even when he was young, he was really diligent about taking care of his body and he was not afraid to ask the vets, like Zydrunas Ilgauskas, who was one of the best in terms of taking care of his body, he was not afraid to ask him what he does daily and then follow his lead. So just an amazing, amazing run for one of the all-time greats.”

On the championship-level upgrade to his travel toiletries kit:

“Something has changed: This is kind of cool. So, our equipment guys are great, Kyle, Steve, Will, shout out to them. One of the best in the league, and they give me a toothbrush and toothpaste, mouthwash, and lotion, and all that. And they put it in my locker area, and they usually just carry it in a paper bag or a plastic bag.

“[Now] they put it in one of those travel things. And they set it really nice on my desk, and I go in there today, and these freaking guys, they made a travel case. Like this is where my lotion is. This is where the Kleenex goes. The two travel Listerines, the deodorant, and Sensodyne toothpaste in the back.

“And, it’s foam. It’s in a case, and not only that, you can’t see it, but right here, it says lotion. Right here, it says deodorant. So this is what championship level coaches get, right? I guarantee Nick [Nurse] has this s–t, too.”

On what he wants from a Knicks contract extension:

“Simply put, I want to do something that can keep the team together and that can work with the Knicks, but also values me. And none of those things have come close to happening.”

On wanting to be paid according to his value after winning a championship and not making concessions:

“No s–t, Sherlock. I just got a championship, you thought it’d be pretty easy… unless you guys think I got anything else to prove?”

On the outlook for reaching an extension before the regular season:

“It don’t look good. I mean in my experience, you just appreciate the moments right now and let it go where it goes.”

On how he is handling the lack of an extension:

On the Knicks’ preseason opener:

“It’s a good first step. Not a great first step, but as long as we’re making strides in the right direction, it’s something to be happy about. Still a lot for us to learn and be better at early”

On Ariel Hukporti’s injury:

“Definitely heartbreaking. When I came back in the locker room, I went to go check on him. Sad to see. Obviously, we’ll pray for him.”

On his first game with the

“It felt good just trying to contribute to the team”

On Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart potentially becoming trade candidates if they remain unsigned:

“Josh Hart has already hinted that, as this gets closer to February, which is around the trade deadline.

“The temperature could rise if Karl-Anthony Towns and Hart himself are not extended. So far, these sides are not close.”

items.title: 76ers 120, Knicks 97: Scenes from a sleepy scrimmage
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Real fans watch preseason games, these half-hearted scrimmages in which stars tend to lollygag, and the guys fighting for roster or rotation consideration tend to play as you’d expect—like guys trying to secure seats at the southern reach of the bench. Bandwagoners and parade crashers don’t tune in for this slop. Real fans do, cuz a Knicks game is a Knicks game. We even watch summer league!

After a short summer respite, the World Champion Knickerbockers and your loyal P&T blogger were all feeling rusty. From the start of tonight’s 120-97 loss to the Sixers, the champs continued to show their penchant for the long ball, heaving more than half their shots from the outfield. Both teams converted 33% from deep through the first 12 minutes, and here’s some good news: Finals MVP Jalen Brunson’s surgically repaired wrist had a familiar sweet snap as he drilled two three-pointers.

The guests took an early lead, but Philly answered with a 14-3 stretch through the heart of the quarter. Seeing former Celtic Jaylen Brown in Philadelphia blue boggled the brain for a moment. He carried his unit with LeBron James, Joel Embiid, and Tyrese Maxey taking the night off (chickens), and the new Sixer collected 13 early points. Meanwhile, Brunson and OG () Anunoby scored eight points apiece for our heroes.

Former Knick Ariel Hukporti started the game, but exited early with an injury after facing up with Karl-Anthony Towns. He was assisted to the locker room, and it had the hallmarks of an Achilles tear. If that turns out to be the case, it’s a devastating blow to a likable guy who stood to get significant playing time this season.

On the subject of Towns, he attacked the paint and looked not a bit sour about his contract situation. Behind him, Andre Drummond played his first (unofficial) game as a Knick and was exactly the same Drummond he’s always been.

As the quarter went on, Tyler Kolek (with longer locks) assumed ball-handling duties. He seemed to have a mandate to score and forced it a little. Due to an absence of defense on either side, the teams swapped buckets like high-schoolers on layup lines. One welcome exception was the dependable Landry Shamet, who drained a pair of triples.

After 13 lead changes, the Knicks finished the quarter trailing just 33-32, despite the Sixers out-shooting them 54% to 48%.

To start the second quarter, Jaylen Brown returned for a short stint, as did Brunson and Towns for the Knicks.

But, true to his word, Coach Mike Brown doled out minutes to as many players as he could. The spotlight in these early days is squarely on sophomore Mohamed Diawara. He attacked the rim with mixed results and coughed up the ball twice. Not a great sign after a crummy summer league. Alongside him, Jordan Clarkson logged his allotment of minutes, picking up where he left off.

Veteran James Wiseman took a turn at center, hoping to convince Brown to award him the team’s final roster spot. He scored two buckets but seemed a step slow on defense. Speaking of which, Pacome Dadiet guarded with more aggression than I remember. His offense, however, was pretty much exactly as I remembered—he and Miles McBride combined to shoot 0-of-4 from downtown in the half.

The second quarter belonged to the 76ers, who reached a 14-point lead late in the period and went into intermission ahead 72-58. They shot 53% from the field and 46% from deep, converting 11 dingers to the Knicks’ five. After missing a bunch of shots in the second quarter, our guys had shot 23% from deep. Brown led all first-half scorers with 22, while Anunoby logged 12 for the good guys.

Kolek and Shamet started the third, as did Walker, who answered their buckets with a trey of his own. Diawara turned on the charm with consecutive finger-rolls, a putback, and a steal. From there, the teams traded inefficient offensive blows.

Drummond swatted three blocks, and his layup fueled a nice push during that run, but Clarkson committed two travel violations and whiffed on multiple shots. Wiseman hit from the line and dunked a tip-in, while Ochai Agbaji went scoreless with some misses, and Dadiet’s fouls sent the Sixers to the stripe. By the end of this sludgefest, both teams had scored 21 points. The Knicks were still down, now 93-79.

Drew Eubanks and Bruce Brown started the fourth quarter for the Knicks, and we saw cameos by Kevin McCullar, Jr., Tyler Nickel, Tony Bradley, and Jaden Akins. By the buzzer, Brown had played 20 players (and it would’ve been 21, but Jose Alvarado is nursing a bruised knee). Aikins and Dadiet both hit from deep, which were rare sights on a night when the Knicks shot 8-of-41 from yard.

For the home team, rookie forward Saint Thomas impressed with a double-double. Thanks to his efforts, the Liberty Bells inflated their lead to 23. Caleb Love continued to have a nice game for them (15 points, 3-of-6 from deep). When the cutting was done, our heroes had fallen, 120-97. Big deal. We’ll give these bums the business on banner night.

The Knicks host the Wizards on Thursday. Safe travels, Knickerbockers, and get well soon, Huk.

items.title: Preseason Game Thread: Knicks at 76ers, October 5, 2026
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Knicks travel to Xfinity Mobile Arena tonight for their inaugural preseason game and their first appearance on the court since beating the Spurs for the NBA Championship (yes, that really happened).

The 76ers are not the same team that New York swept in round two of the playoffs. This offseason, Philly bulked up with additions of Jaylen Brown and LeBron James. Paired with fellow starters Tyrese Maxey, Joel Embiid, and V.J. Edgecombe, this squad is built to challenge the throne. Temper your excitement for tonight’s tilt, though: James, Embiid, and Maxey, Anfernee Simons, Dominick Barlow, Adem Bona, and Tacko Fall are all OUT tonight.

We expect limited minutes for New York’s starters—Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges, Josh Hart, O.G. () Anunoby, and Karl-Anthony Towns—as they continue to get back online after a short summer break. Meanwhile, Coach Mike Brown is eager to see what Mohamed Diawara brings to the table in year two, and who stands out among the centers competing for the third-string spot. Jose Alvarado (knee contusion) is the only Knick on the injury report.

Game time is at 7 p.m. EST on MSG. This is your game thread. This is Liberty Ballers. Please don’t post large photos, GIFs, or links to illegal streams in the thread. Be excellent humans. And go Knicks!

items.title: Monday Posted & Toasted Notes: KAT sounds off, yearning Mike, basketball time!
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Last time I checked, we were celebrating. Turns out, we’re now back to watching games take place again! Not , but hey, the boys can only play when they tell them to, and I won’t complain. Links and things today, quotes (probably) tomorrow.

  • Karl-Anthony Towns made it very clear on Monday morning that he and the New York Knicks aren’t even remotely close to agreeing to a contract extension at this point.

“Simply put, I want to do something to keep the team together and can work with the Knicks and also values me. And none of those things are close to happening.

“(Reaching an agreement before the start of the regular season) doesn’t look good.

“No s–t Sherlock (an extension shouldn’t be understood as a reward for last season). I just won a championship. You’d think it was pretty easy. Unless you guys (reporters) think I have something else to prove.”

  • More on that inside the newsletter, but here’s a summary for the lazy: the Knicks enter the season with the highest preseason over/under win total in the Eastern Conference for the first time since 1993, with sportsbooks setting them around 52.5 to 53.5 wins, but New York has finished with the East’s No. 1 seed only four times in franchise history and hasn’t done it since 1993. Something has to give, doesn’t it?
  • Nitty-gritty breakdown of KAT’s contract situation by The Athletic’s Fred Katz and how it could eventually have major implications for Miles McBride’s future in New York.
  • Carmelo Anthony believes neither LeBron James, Joel Embiid or Jaylen Brown should remain the central figure in Philadelphia after the Sixers’ blockbuster offseason.
  • Giannis Antetokounmpo made it clear he still has “five, six good years” remaining in his career, all of which would probably go for nothing while the Heat remain in cap hell without a strong-enough roster around the Greek. Hooray!
  • Dillon Brooks hopes he has another decade of NBA basketball ahead of him and doesn’t want his “great year” (?) to make him complacent.
  • Old-man-yelling-at-a-cloud Cedric Ceballos argued last year that Stephen Curry wouldn’t have been given the same freedom to launch extremely deep 3-pointers in his era and would never have become a great hooper, let alone the man who changed basketball, and recently explained his take. Not sure it convinces me.

items.title: Preseason Game Preview: Knicks at 76ers, October 5, 2026
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Is there really a game already? Oy vey. We are still getting used to how brief the summer break is when the basketball team you cover is actually successful in the postseason.

Indeed, the NBA champion New York Knicks open their preseason schedule tonight. They’ll travel to face a Philadelphia 76ers club that has bolstered its own championship aspirations this summer. What was a solid but flawed Eastern Conference contender now features LeBron James and Jaylen Brown alongside Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, and sophomore VJ Edgecombe, assembling one of the most star-studliest lineups in the league.

For the defending champions, this scrimmage will be the first peek at what Mike Brown hopes to tweak for the upcoming season. The second-year coach has already stressed that he intends to ease his core into the exhibition slate. They had a short summer recess, after all. Jalen Brunson, Mikal Bridges, Josh Hart, OG () Anunoby, and Karl-Anthony Towns will not shoulder heavy workloads right away, which should open the door for extended looks at the players still fighting for roster security and rotation minutes. Additionally, sophomore Mohamed Diawara will be challenged to prove that he’s ready for a leap after a promising first season and fizzling out in summer league.

We’ll be focused on the center position where the coaching staff is still sorting out depth behind Towns and former Sixer Andre Drummond. Journeymen James Wiseman, Tony Bradley, and Drew Eubanks are all competing in camp for the third-string spot, and Monday’s game affords them a chance to show how they stack up against Embiid and ex-Knick Ariel Hukporti.

As for the health of New York’s starters, Hart continues to play with a damaged digit, and Brunson has reportedly looked sharp in camp after recovering from wrist surgery. Meanwhile, there’s an undercurrent of unresolved contracts, with Towns, Hart, and Miles McBride all eligible for veteran extensions. Because they are in (or effectively in) the final year of their deals—McBride on an expiring contract, Towns with a $61M player option for 2027-28, and Hart with a $22.4M team option for 2027-28—they can negotiate and sign extensions at any point until June 30, 2027. All three have expressed interest in buttoning up their paperwork sooner than that, but this seems like the storyline that will hang over the entire season.

For the Fightin’ Cheesesteaks, our curiosity centers around how coach Nick Nurse will get James, Brown, Embiid, and Maxey to share the ball and defend consistently. We expect their early games to have some of the confusion of an All-Star game, when the alphas try to figure out who will be less-alpha on any given play.

Really, the primary goal of a preseason game is “Don’t break nothin.” You won’t see Captain Brunson take a charge tonight, or Hart do anything that could make his finger fall off. New York swept the Liberty Bells in the second round of the playoffs, as part of a 13-game win streak, and while tonight’s opponent has improved, neither club wants to reveal its tricks in a meaningless contest. They’ll save the good stuff for opening night, when they clash on banner night at Madison Square Garden. Still, it will be fun to see our champs take the floor again. And so soon. Prediction: Knicks by six.

Who: New York Knicks (0-0) at Philadelphia 76ers (0-0)Date: Monday, October 5, 2026Place: Xfinity Mobile Arena (formerly Wells Fargo Center), Philadelphia, PAFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I think he has endless upside’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Paying homage to my biggest brain fart…

Would you believe the Knicks play basketball tomorrow!?

Here’s the latest from around Tarrytown and those places.

On Mohamed Diawara’s increased comfort and development entering Year 2:

“Last year, you could see he was a little jittery when he was out there, because he didn’t quite know what to do, and he knew when he did it, he just had to go hard. So a lot of times, he would just play at one speed. There’s a comfort level now, so his cadence is better, especially offensively. His ability to communicate on the floor is at a little bit of a higher level, because he has a better feel not just offensively, but defensively — not just what he should do, but what he should be telling his teammates to do, especially if he’s on the backside or bottom side of the defense, because he sees everything in front of him. He’s one of those players that needs to take a step forward.”

On his plans for the preseason opener:

“(Starters will play,) but not much. We’ll try to ease them in. The last game is always a dress rehearsal, but we’ll try to build them up leading to that game.”

On accepting preseason mistakes and emphasizing next-play speed:

“Any time you have new guys, because we have new guys on this team that we’re trying to mix in with guys that have been here, you’re gonna make some mistakes. I’m 100 percent OK with that. Once somebody makes a mistake, I’m looking for how quickly do they try to make up for the same mistake? I’m huge on the next-play speed.

“So there’s gonna be a a lot of mistakes, but are guys gonna drop their head a little or hesitate? It happened anyway. Move on, try to correct it. and then address it during the day also.”

On what he’ll prioritize seeing in preseason:

“Overall effort, the little things like boxing out every single time, competing, offensively, to offensive rebound, and then sprinting corner-to-corner in transition.”

On ending practices with a must-make free throw:

“It puts pressure on guys, you know, and then everybody’s standing there watching. So if you miss it, everybody’s got to run. I got it from Pop. It also, at the end of the day, brings the group together.”

On Tony Bradley making the final free throw on Saturday:

“You see everybody came and gave him love. So you feel good when you do it.”

On being followed home by a family of Knicks fans after the championship:

“I stopped at the red light. The first vehicle was kind of honking at me and I could see the kids waving out. So I go through and they turn into a driveway three or four houses past the red light and the father and kids jump out of the car and start waving and they had their Knicks gear on and I gave them a wave.

“But I had my helmet and my sunglasses, so I didn’t think anybody noticed me. So I ride home and I’ve got my country music blasting, and I pull into my driveway in my garage, and the next thing you know, that car was pulling into my driveway. They followed me home.

“I don’t know how they got back in their car that quickly and followed me home. But they followed me home. And the guy owns a company and he had some food products, so he brings out a box of cereal and all that. And he’s got his three kids and they just start telling me what the championship meant . . .

“This is like August, two months after the championship, but you could still feel that passion. So was it scary? Yes. It was scary. Any time you get followed home, it is very, very scary, but just to see the joy and excitement, especially on kids’ faces.

“The dad was more excited than the kids, by the way, but to see that, you realize this is not just a championship. This is special.”

On falling out of the Knicks’ rotation during his rookie season:

“Honestly, It didn’t really need explanation. I think I was a rookie. That was my first year. So you just got to be ready, whatever the team wants you to do. We have a great team with big players, so if I was in the rotation and I’m not in the rotation anymore, I think it’s just part of the game for the whole team. I wasn’t really thinking about that, I was just ready to take any opportunity. I wasn’t thinking about not playing and stuff.”

On better understanding how to prepare his body for the NBA:

“Now that I know a little bit more the physicality that I need in the league, how I need to prepare my body. … I think now that I have a year in the league, it’s a little bit easier to see how I can prepare for the new season.”

On the Knicks’ championship parade and his offseason:

“I always knew Knicks fans were another kind of fans…I was prepared for it to be a big thing. But I was surprised, it was great to see.

“Best summer of my life… went back to Paris, it was nice. Everybody was happy about it.”

On Mohamed Diawara’s potential:

“I think he has endless upside. He’s very talented, can do a lot: shoot, defend, pass. He can do everything; a really versatile player. I’m excited to see him grow. I think he’s going to keep getting better and better, so I’m really excited for him.”

On receiving the key to his hometown of Jefferson City:

“Yeah, they just told me they were going to do it. I grew up in Jeff City, went to high school out there, have lifelong friends, and I just — I grew up there.

“So Jeff City, Missouri is special to me. So it’s an honor.”

On believing more recognition will come after the Knicks’ championship run:

“Throughout the season, that’s where more recognition will come. This next season, I think I put it on display every night, the versatility, being able to guard anyone and affect the game offensively and defensively. I’m a two-way player, that’s what I take pride in, helping the team win games. I think I’ve always done it.

“Maybe there’s more of an eye on it right now because we just won the championship. That’s what I pride myself in.”

On Mike Brown’s coaching chops:

“He deserves all the praise… he’s always been a great coach. When you win, you get more recognition. Everything is coming together for him.”

On his work with Pacome Dadiet and Mo:

“I encourage them when they’re doing well… be there for them any way I can.”

“It was fun, we were there for Jalen. Was really cool that he got to host it. We were there for the intro. It was cool to see him do that, some funny skits. It was a good time.”

On not falling for his flowers:

“I really do appreciate it and I respect the hell out of them. It’s honestly really cool and it’s a sign of respect. To hear that from those guys, I really do appreciate it.

“It’s just like a lot of things. When you hear praise, when you hear negativity, it has to go through one ear and out the other. You got to continue to be the best version of yourself or people are going to pass you. I really do appreciate it. It shows where I’ve grown, but still got a lot of work to do.”

items.title: Saturday Posted & Toasted Notes: Wise men, French presidents, BrickBron James
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Last weekend without basketball, fellas, so here’s a quick summary of a bunch of stuff that popped up recently around the NBA before we get down to (yeah, I know, , but still…) business.

  • James Wiseman has emerged as the early favorite for the Knicks’ 14th and likely final standard roster spot, according to the New York Post’s Stefan Bondy. Nothing new considering we’ve been talking about New York prioritizing a third center for months on end. In Bondy’s eyes, Tony Bradley and Drew Eubanks are Wiseman’s primary competition up front, while Bruce Brown and Ochai Agbaji are also fighting for the last spot in the Knicks’ roster.
  • Mike Brown, however, isn’t ready to declare Wiseman—or anybody else—the winner of that roster battle.

“I’m just going to let it unfold. I got no expectations. I’m not trying to forecast anything. I’m just taking this literally one practice at a time, one game at a time. And at the end of the day, when it comes time for us to figure out who’s going to be on the final roster, we’ll do it.”

  • The Athletic’s James L. Edwards III identified whether the Knicks can maintain their edge after winning the championship as New York’s biggest question entering the new season.
  • In another piece published over The Athletic, multiple reporters assembled three perspectives on the Knicks’ chances of repeating, and none were especially bullish.
  • Anne Hathaway would sacrifice another Oscar for another Knicks championship.
  • The Pistons and Jalen Duren finally found common ground, with the big boy and postseason no-shower inking a five-year, $200 million deal… without a weight clause on it.
  • Victor Wembanyama hasn’t even won an NBA title, but he’s already thinking about running for President of France.
  • It looks like the Las Vegas Whatevers are a very real thing and will get a franchise approved before Seattle does, but that could come with the con of having to wait an extra year to enter NBA play, contrary to the SuperSonics 2.0 making their comeback in time for the 2028-29 campaign.
  • JaVale McGee has joined the Shanghai Sharks, teaming up with D’Angelo Russell in China. Yes, that’s a real headline.
  • LeBron stans are already aboard the #lbjmvp train. Meanwhile…

items.title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘Either joint replacement, let it go, or, I guess, amputation’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
My brain melted yesterday, thought it was Sunday, not Thursday.

Anyway, today’s Friday. I guess.

Here’s the latest from Tarrytown as we keep hearing from different Knicks.

On Josh Hart’s injured finger and the toughness it reflects:

“Josh, he’s a handsome young man. But that finger is ugly. So, I don’t look at it. But it adds to his toughness. Josh is a tough son of a gun, man. I can’t even watch when he [shakes his hand], because I’m just like, oh, my gosh I can’t imagine having a finger like that.

“But it just shows who he is. He’s tough but, more importantly, there’s dedication there to wanting to be a great shooter, and you’ve got to put it into work. And he puts in the work, even though his finger’s bothering him. And even though it’s a little crooked, he’s putting in the work to get it right. [Shooting coach] Pete [Patton] and the rest of the coaches are helping him out, and it shows that he can shoot at a high level with the dedication he has in the first place.”

On OG Anunoby’s playoff performance boosting his All-Star case:

“It should help him a ton because guys that are quiet naturally, they have a hard time getting the necessary publicity and promotion toward being an All-Star, unless you’re doing something extraordinary and people start talking about it — like OG in the playoffs. So doing it in the playoffs and having people talk about it should have carryover, in my opinion, since he helped us win the championship.

“And he was in the conversation for [NBA] Finals MVP. That should definitely help create calls for him to have a case to be an All-Star this year. He’s still got to go earn it, but he should be in everybody’s conversation from the beginning.”

On Anunoby’s shooting ability:

“He’s not [at Stephen Curry] or [Klay Thompson’s] level but the next tier. He’s way better than I thought.”

On Anunoby’s confidence, shooting and the Knicks’ spacing:

“His confidence is really high. And I thought during the playoffs we did a really good job of touching the paint and taking the right 3s. With OG being 6-foot-7 with long arms, if you’re closing to him with a smaller guy or a guard, it’s going to be good for us because they try to put their best player on Jalen, and sometimes, their best player is a bigger perimeter defender.

“So that means OG may have a smaller guy [defending him]. That’s not impacting him when he shoots the basketball.

“So I think first starts off with him, yes; he’s way better than what I thought. I would categorize him as a great shooter. But more importantly, I thought our spacing and our ability to touch the paint and spray it helped out a lot.”

On his plans for the preseason games:

“We’ll try to ease them in. The last game is always a dress rehearsal, but we’ll try to build them up leading to that game.”

On the Knicks’ conditioning entering camp after a short summer:

“All the guys look like they’re in pretty good shape, especially for a short summer. We have a conditioning test that we did last year and this year that the guys have to pass to get into camp and they all passed it.”

On James Wiseman’s presence at training camp:

“Fantastic human being, fantastic young man…. Good to see him in the gym. When you’re that long and that athletic, with skill – he has skill – there’s a place for you in this league. Sometimes it takes the right moment, the right team, the right situation, all that stuff, to be able to fit someplace and grow. We have a lot of great guys in camp that have potential of impacting us in a lot of different ways throughout the course of the year. He’s definitely one of the many guys that we have that we’re excited about.”

On Tony Bradley after his training camp signing:

“We’re looking for bigs. Tony’s a veteran guy that’s still in his prime and has a good feel for the game, knows how to play the game the right way and he’s hurt us in the past. To be honest, when a guy hurts you in the past, you tend to remember him more than others. So to be able to add him to camp was a positive for us because again, I said this last year, (Karl-Anthony Towns) has one of the most (challenging positions) out of everybody because I want to move him around when I play him at center. I want to play him at power forward; (when he’s at) power forward 1-4 is interchangeable. Same with OG (Anunoby). OG we put him at the 5 last year. We probably will do it a little bit more this year as well.

“But to be able to do that, you’ve gotta have enough centers around on the team, so having Tony here with his skill set and feel is definitely a blessing because we’re looking at that position heavily.”

On the options to fix his finger:

“The only option for my finger at this point, because of how damaged it is, is a full joint replacement. With a joint replacement, you can’t have the banging, grabbing a rebound, palming it, shooting, catching the ball, doing all that. You can’t do that. So if I did a joint replacement, then I wouldn’t be able to play. So I guess it’s either wrap it until I retire or cut it off. I guess that’s the other option. That’s really the only alternative: either joint replacement, let it go, or, I guess, amputation.

“I mean, there was a lot of stuff that I had to get checked, and that was one of them. It was just with how it deteriorated, the joint and the bone and everything, that’s what it’ll be. So I’ll do that probably when I retire. Hopefully, they can make it straight. You know, it’s a little off center if y’all didn’t realize. So I’m hoping after that joint replacement it can kind of get a little straighter.”

On how the pain in his finger varies from day to day:

“Some days, it’ll be good. Some days it’ll hurt to catch the ball. It varies. I wish I could tell you when I wake up what’s gonna be good, what’s gonna be bad. Somedays it’s good, like a regular functioning finger. And other days it hurts to just close my hand, to make a fist.”

On why a joint replacement would prevent him from playing basketball:

“You can’t have the banging, you know, repetitive, grabbing a rebound, palming it, shooting, catching the ball, doing all that; you can’t do that. It was just with how it deteriorated — the joint and the bone and everything — that’s what it’ll be. So I’ll do that probably when I retire. Hopefully they can make it straight. You know, it’s a little off center if you know y’all didn’t realize.”

On the appearance and functionality of his injured finger:

“I mean, it’s it’s not the prettiest to look at. I would love to have a straight finger, but you know, it works.”

On the physical toll of an NBA career and what fans don’t get:

“I think people think money is everything, and for me, obviously, you want to be compensated fairly for your performance and all that. But at the end of the day, just because you get paid, be blessed in a position to get paid well and take care of our families, [it’s not like] we’re not humans at the same time. I’m sitting here thinking, my knees are aching a little bit, but I want to leave the game and be able to run around and play with my kids when they’re you know 10, 11,12-plus. So that wear and tear, it’s significant to a certain point. If you’re in this league for 14, 15, 16 years, and you see some of these guys that are older, they they got limps, knees are barking, those kind of things. So I think that definitely gets overlooked. But that’s also why I don’t think I’ll play till I’m 40.”

On OG Anunoby’s increased recognition helping his All-Star chances:

“It’s extremely impactful. Obviously, you have to be a gifted and good player to make an All-Star team, but also you have to have the press and all that kind of behind you, bolstering it. So it’s good for people to see how talented he is, how impactful he is on both sides of the ball in the game. So hopefully that recognition will continue throughout this year, and hopefully we’ll be able to get him in.”

On Jalen Brunson’s increased fame following the Knicks title:

“He’s not LeBron, let’s relax.”

On planning to attend Yankees Game 3:

“I think I’m going to be able to get to Game 3. We have a preseason game the next day. So I’m excited, man. I’m excited for New York. Excited for that team.”

On OG Anunoby’s playoff success boosting his confidence:

“That’s definitely a boost of confidence going into this year. OG knows how good he is, and we know how good he is. So he’s gonna continue doing what he does.”

On learning the backcourt rule during his late Game 4 possession:

“I learned on the fly. When I watched the video after, they said you can leave the ball in the backcourt but your body can be in the frontcourt – I didn’t know it was a thing until then. I’m glad it worked out.”

On what has allowed the Knicks to embrace their roles:

“We care for each other, we compete, we want to get each other better”

On whether he always planned to return to the Knicks before signing his extension:

“In my mind, yeah. ‘I want to stay here, I want to stay home.’ We had a chance to do that, and we did it.”

On his championship summer:

“My favorite summer of all time”

items.title: On This Date in Knicks History: October 2
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Two noteworthy Knicks birthdays today!

Dr. Dick Barnett was born October 2, 1936, in Gary, Indiana. Barnett spent eight seasons with New York, became an All-Star in 1968, and played for both the 1970 and 1973 championship teams. His number 12 hangs in the Garden rafters. He died last year at 88.

Barnett had one of the most unforgettable shots in basketball history. Starting in college (when nicknamed “Dick the Skull”), he became known for contorting his body into a question mark while shooting his jumper, kicking his legs back and telling defenders, “Too late–fall back, baby!” Barnett went on to turn his eccentric shot into more than 15,000 NBA points.

A beloved teammate of Walt Frazier, Barnett was featured in the documentary film, , about his time playing at Tennessee State University for the Tigers. During segregation, the all-Black Tigers won three straight national championships. Captain Barnett tirelessly fought for their recognition, which culminated in their 2019 induction into the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame. Watch the doc here, you’ll dig it.

After hanging up his sneakers, Barnett earned an MBA from New York University and then a PhD in education from Fordham University. He taught Sports Management at St. John’s University for four years.

  • 2× NBA champion (1970, 1973)
  • All-ABL First Team (1962)
  • No. 12 retired by New York Knicks
  • 3× NAIA champion (1957–1959)
  • 3× AP Little College All-American (1957–1959)
  • 2× UPI Little College All-American (1958, 1959)
  • 2× NAIA tournament MVP (1958, 1959)

And (feeling like Garrison Keillor here) Tyson Chandler was born today in 1982, in Hanford, California. Chandler came to New York immediately after anchoring Dallas’ 2011 championship defense and became the 2011-12 NBA Defensive Player of the Year, the only Knick ever to take the honor.

Drafted second in 2001, the seven-foot Chandler played for five seasons in Chicago before bouncing from NOLA to Charlotte to Dallas and then the Knicks. After three seasons at MSG, he was sent back to Dallas, then Phoenix, and finished out his 19-year career with the Lakers and Rockets.

Chandler joined the Knicks in December 2011 via a sign-and-trade between multiple teams, which also sent traded Ronny Turiaf, cash, and a 2013 2nd-round draft pick to the Wizards. While there was no denying his talent, Chandler appeared on the injured list often during his tenure here, with a hamstring strain, playoff flu and an upper respiratory infection, a bulging cervical disc (plus related neck spasms and weight loss from illness), and a fractured right fibula.

In June 2014, he and Raymond Felton were traded to the Mavs for José Calderón, Samuel Dalembert, Wayne Ellington, Shane Larkin, a 2014 2nd-round draft pick (Thanasis Antetokounmpo was later selected), and a 2014 2nd-round draft pick (Cleanthony Early was later selected). (h/t basketball-reference.com)

Chandler concluded his time in New York with averages of 10.2 points, 10.1 rebounds, and 1.2 blocks across 183 games. His career highlights, also from Wikipedia:

  • All-NBA Third Team (2012)
  • NBA Defensive Player of the Year (2012)
  • NBA All-Defensive First Team (2013)
  • 2× NBA All-Defensive Second Team (2011, 2012)
  • First-team Parade All-American (2001)
  • Second-team Parade All-American (2000)
  • McDonald’s All-American (2001)
  • 2× California Mr. Basketball (2000, 2001)

Quite a nice pairing: two Knicks born 46 years apart, one remembered for his offense, the other for defense. Closing my Writer’s Almanac loop, your poem for the day is a personal favorite, “The Bear,” by Galway Kinnell.

Knicks in five. And keep in touch.
